items.title: Reds & Blues : Romain Coudrier prend la route pour interroger le malaise américain
items.content:
EN IMAGES

Reds & Blues : Romain Coudrier prend la route pour interroger le malaise américain

En 2025, le photographe français Romain Coudrier a traversé 1 000 kilomètres de Bible Belt américaine en autostop, de Selma à Chicago, pour interroger la polarisation du pays à travers une bichromie rouge et bleu qui donne son titre à la série « Reds & Blues ».


Par Guénola Pellen. Photos de Romain Coudrier. 

Rien ne prédestinait Romain Coudrier à traverser cette ceinture d’États américains, terre de protestantisme évangélique où l’église et l’armurerie se disputent souvent le même parking. En 2025, il se rend à Selma, en Alabama, pour y présenter sa série « Bifröst », consacrée aux paysages du Grand Nord norvégien, récompensée aux Nuits Photographiques de Pierrevert. L’œuvre est exposée une semaine durant à Selma. De là, il aurait pu rentrer sagement mais préfère prolonger son séjour de deux semaines pour rejoindre un ami à Chicago. « Un bon prétexte pour rencontrer les Américains sur la route », résume-t-il.

L’autostop n’a rien d’un caprice de circonstance. C’est une méthode de travail qu’il pratique depuis des années, déjà éprouvée pendant les neuf mois de « Heimat », sur les routes d’Europe, dans la tradition du photojournalisme gonzo, où il s’agit de « laisser [sa] propre expérience devenir la matière même du récit ». Un mythe qu’il voulait éprouver, dit-il, « en déconstruisant [ses] propres idées préconçues, héritées de certains livres beatniks ».

Sur la route, chaque conducteur qui s’arrête devient un sujet potentiel. Il photographie ceux qui le prennent en stop, mais aussi les employés de motel, les serveurs et les SDF croisés en chemin, « du moment qu’il y a une connexion », précise-t-il. Sur le protocole des portraits, la règle est nette. « Il n’y a pas de négociation. Je présente ce que je fais, je demande, c’est oui ou c’est non et on s’en tient là. Généralement, c’est oui », ajoute-t-il. « J’ai eu de rares déconvenues ; uniquement avec des personnes auxquelles je n’avais rien demandé ».

Le parti pris colorimétrique de la série répond à une géographie précise : du Sud vers le Nord, des États rouges, réputés acquis aux Républicains, vers les États bleus, votant Démocrate, ce choix calque le glissement politique du territoire traversé. « J’avais à cœur d’installer une évolution entre le début et la fin de la série et cette bichromie s’est rapidement imposée », explique-t-il. Une fois sur le terrain, ce motif le rattrape partout, des maillots de sport aux pailles de fast-food : « C’est devenu une obsession ». L’évolution introspective du voyage, de la tension à un désarroi plus amer, fixe finalement la palette de ses tirages en « rouges urines » et « bleu gaz ».

Dès les premiers kilomètres, Romain Coudrier est catalogué par ses interlocuteurs comme marginal, soit, dans ce contexte, indésirable voire dangereux. « J’ai donc, en premier lieu, affaire à la peur des autres, une peur d’abord surprenante, puis pénible, et qui a fini par m’assombrir », confie-t-il. « Je fais face à des regards et des postures bien différents selon que j’achète un sandwich en caisse ou que je m’approche de quelqu’un qui fait le plein d’essence. J’ai pourtant le même sac à dos, le même imperméable et le même accent à couper au couteau ».

Quant à l’imaginaire criminel qui traverse la série, il revendique une ignorance de départ. « Cela m’est bien étranger », concède-t-il à propos des figures connues de la criminalité routière, avant de mesurer combien cet imaginaire, daté mais toujours vivace, sert quotidiennement d’alibi au refus. D’où l’intégration de rapports policiers, dossiers judiciaires et articles de presse locale, mêlés à des objets glanés sur la route.

« Reds & Blues » n’instruit aucun procès. « Ce n’est pas une critique des individus, mais le constat de l’influence d’une structure sur les individus », insiste-t-il. « Le conformisme n’est jamais loin et il est facile de faire la morale derrière son appareil photo ». La série, nuance-t-il, « n’est pas une série anti-américaine : elle interroge un lien social conditionné, voire détérioré, par des mécaniques qui dépassent la nationalité ou la croyance ».

Le plus dur à négocier se joue en lui-même, dans l’asymétrie entre son statut de voyageur temporaire et la précarité durable de certains qu’il croise, avec lesquels un malentendu de circonstance a pu le confondre, lui aussi posté au bord du chemin avec sa pancarte. « Je viens, je parle, j’écoute, je retourne dans mon monde. » C’est à eux, précise-t-il, qu’il dédie cette série.

Instagram : @romain.coudrier

items.title: Reds & Blues: Romain Coudrier Takes to the Road to Question America’s Malaise
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Reds & Blues: Romain Coudrier Takes to the Road to Question America's Malaise

In 2025, French photographer Romain Coudrier hitchhiked 1,000 kilometres across the American Bible Belt, from Selma to Chicago, to examine the country’s polarization through a red-and-blue duotone that gives the series its title, “Reds & Blues.”

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Romain Coudrier. 

Nothing destined Romain Coudrier to cross this belt of states, an evangelical Protestant country where the church and the gun shop often share the same parking lot. In 2025, he travels to Selma, Alabama, to present his series “Bifröst,” devoted to the landscapes of Norway’s Far North, awarded at the Nuits Photographiques de Pierrevert. The work is exhibited for a week in Selma. From there, he could have gone home. Instead, he extends his stay by two weeks to visit a friend in Chicago. “A good pretext to meet Americans on the road,” he sums up.

Hitchhiking is no accident of circumstance. It is a working method he has practiced for years, already tested during the nine months of “Heimat,” on the roads of Europe, within the tradition of gonzo photojournalism, where the aim is to “let [his] own experience become the very material of the narrative.” An American myth he wanted to test, he says, “by dismantling [his] own preconceived ideas, inherited from certain beatnik books.”

On the road, every driver who stops becomes a potential subject. He photographs those who pick him up, but also motel clerks, waiters, and homeless people met along the way, “as long as there’s a connection,” he specifies. On the protocol for these portraits, the rule is clear. “There’s no negotiation. I explain what I’m doing, I ask, it’s yes or no, and that’s that. Usually, it’s yes,” he adds. “I had few disappointments, only with people I hadn’t asked.”

The series’ colour scheme reflects a precise geography: heading north from the south, from red states, presumed to lean Republican, to blue states, voting Democrat, this choice mirrors the political drift of the territory crossed. “I wanted to build an evolution from the beginning to the end of the series, and this duotone quickly imposed itself,” he explains. Once on the ground, this pattern confronts him everywhere, from sports jerseys to fast-food straws: “It became an obsession.” The introspective arc of the journey, from tension to a more bitter disillusionment, ultimately fixes the palette of his prints into “piss red” and “gas blue.”

Almost from the first mile, Romain Coudrier is branded by those he meets as an outsider, which in this context means unwelcome, even dangerous. “So my first encounter is with other people’s fear, a fear that was surprising at first, then wearing, and which ended up weighing on me,” he confides. “I’m met with very different looks and postures depending on whether I’m buying a sandwich at the register or approaching someone filling up their tank. Yet I have the same backpack, the same raincoat, the same unmistakable accent.”

As for the criminal imagery running through the series, he admits to an initial ignorance. “That’s quite foreign to me,” he concedes, regarding well-known figures of American road crime, before coming to grasp how much this imagery, dated but still very much alive, serves daily as an alibi for refusal. Hence the inclusion of police reports, court files, and local press clippings, mixed with objects gathered along the road.

“Reds & Blues” passes no verdict. “This isn’t a critique of individuals, but an observation of how a structure shapes individuals,” he insists. “Conformism is never far off, and it’s easy to moralize from behind a camera.” The series, he clarifies, “isn’t an anti-American series: it questions a social bond that is conditioned, even damaged, by mechanisms that go beyond nationality or belief.”

The hardest thing to reconcile plays out within himself, in what he calls a bourgeois-bohemian relationship to the road: “I show up, I talk, I listen, I go back to my world.” He meets people from every social class along the way, some of them in situations of extreme precarity, with whom a chance misunderstanding may have confused him, himself standing roadside with his own sign. “The series is dedicated to them.”

items.title: Joel-Peter Witkin : « Tout le monde est un monstre »
items.content:
On n’entre pas chez Witkin sans un frisson. Depuis son atelier d’Albuquerque, au Nouveau-Mexique, le photographe né à Brooklyn en 1939, a bâti une œuvre dont cette exposition californienne rassemble les images les plus célèbres aux côtés de tirages plus rares, dessinant la trajectoire d’un artiste résolument inclassable.

The Raft of George W. Bush (NM, 2006) en offre une insolente démonstration. Witkin y détourne le célèbre Radeau de la Méduse de Géricault pour y faire voguer l’ancien président, sa mère Barbara, ainsi que Condoleezza Rice, alors secrétaire d’État, l’ancien vice-président  Dick Cheney et Colin Powell, ex secrétaire d’État, saisis dans des postures comiques et peu flatteuses. L’artiste y voit « une nef des fous contemporaine », où un ange « tient un gros os représentant le capitalisme cannibale ».

Sous le provocateur se cache un forcené du travail. Avant de photographier des corps, Joel-Peter Witkin a exercé sa pratique dans l’armée américaine. Doté d’un solide bagage académique, un double master en arts et en beaux-arts, il porte une attention presque architecturale à la matière. Chacune de ses images naît d’un temps long revendiqué. Pour ses compositions, l’artiste construit des scènes de studio entières, bâties à partir de décors peints, d’accessoires symboliques et de figures méticuleusement chorégraphiées dans la filiation des maîtres espagnols de la peinture : Goya, Velázquez et Picasso.

Cette minutie du décorum trouve son prolongement dans son refus obstiné de la retouche numérique. Witkin, qui travaille exclusivement à l’argentique, préfère soumettre ses négatifs et ses tirages à une manipulation physique intense – grattage, déchirure, blanchiment, encaustique, dessin à la main, rehauts de couleur – ce qui confère à ses clichés une texture dense, à mi-chemin entre l’image et la peinture. Le collage, une autre de ses marottes, fait jaillir un visage cubiste d’un fouillis de matières dans Picasso In Purgatory (NM, 2015), comme dans un rêve.

L’humour est rarement absent. Chez Witkin, il flirte avec le sacrilège. Hitler Posing with The Anti-Christ, 1937 (Maquette, NM, 2015) en est une preuve supplémentaire, mêlant grotesque et Histoire avec une désinvolture qui n’exclut jamais la gravité. C’est cette alliance qui donne à son œuvre sa tension si particulière, où l’on rit un instant avant que le malaise ne reprenne ses droits.

Ses natures mortes subversives, peuplées de corps singuliers disposés dans des poses empruntées à la peinture classique, ne cherchent pourtant pas la provocation gratuite, se défend-il. « J’ai toujours détesté le terme “freak show” parce que tout le monde est un monstre », déclare Joel-Peter Witkin dans un discours à la Maison européenne de la photographie à Paris. Le photographe choisit ses modèles, qu’il recrute par petites annonces ou au fil de ses rencontres, avec une rigueur presque cléricale, sélectionnant des êtres que la nature a distingués pour les élever au rang de sujets picturaux, comme dans Studio of the Painter (Courbet), Paris, 1990, ou The Graces, LA, 1988.

« Nous sommes tous sur terre pour sublimer notre spiritualité, notre mental et notre physique, par l’amour désintéressé et par la conviction que nous sommes réellement citoyens d’un autre monde, du Ciel », poursuit Joel-Peter Witkin qui, à ses débuts, avait pour ambition de peindre Dieu. Cette foi affleure dans Nature Sees the First Human Death, Mexico, 2017, et dans Christ Dismissing The Fashionable Artists From The Temple of Art, NN, 2017, où la religion, la mythologie et la mort reviennent sans jamais se réduire à des accessoires de décor. 

Les corps marginalisés qu’il met en scène bousculent les idées reçues sur la normalité, la sainteté et la représentation. L’attraction et la répulsion s’y tiennent en équilibre précaire, un équilibre que l’on retrouve dans Imperfect Thirst (NM, 2016) et The Soul Has No Gender (Mexico, 2016), deux portraits où l’ambiguïté du genre et de l’identité revêt des atours poétiques.

Entrées depuis longtemps dans les collections du MoMA, du Centre Pompidou et du MET, ses photographies gardent intacte leur capacité à déranger. Joel-Peter Witkin sera par ailleurs intronisé en 2026 à l’International Photography Hall of Fame, où il se verra décerner le Visionary Award. 

C’est peut-être là le tour de force de l’artiste : avoir bâti une œuvre adoubée par les institutions tout en résistant au consensus. À Los Angeles, cet été, elle n’a rien perdu de son mordant.

« Joel-Peter Witkin: Selected Works 1973-2018 » est à voir jusqu’au 26 septembre 2026 à la Fahey/Klein Gallery de Los Angeles.

items.title: Joel-Peter Witkin: “Everyone Is a Freak”
items.content:
You don’t walk into a Witkin show without a shiver. From his studio in Albuquerque, New Mexico, the photographer, born in Brooklyn in 1939, has built a body of work that this California exhibition gathers in its most celebrated images, alongside rarer prints, tracing the arc of a career that resists easy categories.

The Raft of George W. Bush (NM, 2006) offers the most audacious proof of it. Witkin hijacks Géricault’s famous Raft of the Medusa to set adrift the former president, his mother Barbara, along with Condoleezza Rice, then Secretary of State, former Vice President Dick Cheney, and Colin Powell, a former Secretary of State, caught in comic and unflattering poses. The artist calls it “a contemporary ‘Ship of Fools,'” in which an angel “holds a large bone signifying cannibalistic capitalism, that charnel house of our dismal social progress.”

Beneath the provocateur lurks a relentless worker. Before photographing bodies, Joel-Peter Witkin served as a photographer in the US Army. Armed with formidable academic credentials, a double master’s degree in arts and fine arts, he brings an almost architectural attention to matter itself. Each image is born of a deliberately unhurried process. For his compositions, the artist builds entire studio scenes from painted backdrops, symbolic props, and meticulously choreographed figures, in the lineage of the great Spanish masters of painting: Goya, Velázquez, and Picasso.

This devotion to decorum carries through in his stubborn refusal of digital retouching. Witkin, who works exclusively on film, prefers to subject his negatives and prints to intense physical manipulation, scratching, tearing, bleaching, encaustic, hand-drawing, hand-tinting, giving his images a dense texture that sits somewhere between photograph and painting. Collage, another of his obsessions, conjures a cubist face out of a tangle of materials in Picasso In Purgatory (NM, 2015), as if pulled from a dream.

Humor is rarely absent. In Witkin’s hands, it flirts with sacrilege. Hitler Posing with The Anti-Christ, 1937 (Maquette, NM, 2015) is further proof, blending the grotesque and history with a nonchalance that never excludes gravity. It’s this pairing that gives his work its particular tension, where laughter arrives a beat before unease reclaims its ground.


His subversive still lifes, populated with singular bodies arranged in poses borrowed from classical painting, aren’t after cheap provocation, he insists. “I’ve always hated the term ‘freak show’ because everyone is a freak,” Witkin once declared in a speech at the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. The photographer selects his models, whom he recruits through classified ads or chance encounters, with an almost clerical rigor, seeking out beings that nature has singled out and elevating them to the rank of pictorial subjects, as in Studio of the Painter (Courbet), Paris, 1990, or The Graces, LA, 1988.

“We’re on earth because we all must overcome our spiritual, mental, and physical; by ‘unselfish’ love, and by the faith that we’re really citizens of another world — of Heaven,” Witkin continued, a man who, early on, had set out to paint God. That faith surfaces in Nature Sees the First Human Death, Mexico, 2017, and in Christ Dismissing The Fashionable Artists From The Temple of Art, NN, 2017, where religion, mythology, and death keep returning without ever becoming mere set dressing.

The marginalized bodies he stages upend received ideas about normalcy, holiness, and representation. Attraction and repulsion hold each other in precarious balance, an equilibrium found again in Imperfect Thirst (NM, 2016) and The Soul Has No Gender (Mexico, 2016), two portraits in which the ambiguity of gender and identity takes on poetic form.


Long since held in the collections of MoMA, the Centre Pompidou and the Met, his photographs have lost none of their capacity to unsettle. Joel-Peter Witkin will also be inducted into the International Photography Hall of Fame in 2026, where he will receive the Visionary Award.

That may be the artist’s real feat: building a body of work embraced by institutions while still resisting consensus. In Los Angeles this summer, it still bites.

“Joel-Peter Witkin: Selected Works 1973-2018” runs through September 26, 2026 at the Fahey/Klein Gallery, in Los Angeles.

items.title: Du calotype au pixel, 200 ans de photographie écossaise
items.content:
EN IMAGES

Du calotype au pixel, 200 ans de photographie écossaise

À l’image de ce cliché de Wendy McMurdo, la photographie écossaise n’a cessé de trafiquer le réel pour mieux raconter son pays. Cet été, Dalkeith Palace, résidence historique des ducs de Buccleuch aux portes d’Édimbourg, retrace deux siècles de ce médium, des calotypes pionniers de Hill & Adamson jusqu’aux pratiques documentaires d’aujourd’hui, à l’occasion du bicentenaire de la Royal Scottish Academy (RSA). Tour d’horizon en images des photographes exposés.

Par Guénola Pellen. Photos : avec l’aimable autorisation de PhotoDalkeith RSA200

Devant ses propres tableaux de tulipes, Derrick Guild peint en direct des motifs décoratifs sur des tulipes vivantes. Follower documente cette performance donnée lors de l’Exposition Annuelle de la RSA en 2016, où l’artiste endosse le rôle d’un suiveur de l’Âge d’or hollandais. La scène rejoue la tulipomanie, quand une fleur valait dix fois le salaire annuel d’un artisan qualifié. Formé à l’école d’art Duncan of Jordanstone, à Dundee, Derrick Guild peint depuis des natures mortes hantées par les maîtres flamands et hollandais.

Daniel Cook s’immerge dans la vie de ses sujets pour un cinéma aussi documentaire que fictionnel, donnant voix à des communautés dont les histoires restent trop souvent tues. Ricky Babes appartient à sa série « Love Letters From Aberdeenshire ». Lauréat du Morton Award de la RSA en 2019, il vit et travaille à Glasgow.

Un fragment de nature enrubanné de brins d’herbe et de toile d’araignée, presque abstrait à force de gros plan. Matthew Dalziel et Louise Scullion collaborent depuis 1993, sculptant, filmant et photographiant une nature en mutation. Leur installation Migrator, conçue en 1997 pour l’aéroport de Heathrow, reste l’une de leurs commandes publiques les plus marquantes. Le duo écrit vouloir « renouer sensuellement le corps humain à la terre élémentaire ».

Le visage grimé de l’artiste, entre autoportrait et mascarade, incarne ce Self Portrait of Us All as the Devil. Graham Fagen a représenté l’Écosse à la Biennale de Venise en 2015 avec The Slave’s Lament, installation vidéo mêlant un poème de Robert Burns et la voix du chanteur reggae Ghetto Priest. Esclavage, influences musicales, pouvoir symbolique des fleurs : ses œuvres, souvent développées dans la durée avec d’autres collaborateurs, interrogent sans relâche l’identité nationale et personnelle.

Une étendue d’eau agitée, saisie en pleine tempête, brouille l’horizon entre ciel et mer. Depuis 1984, Thomas Joshua Cooper remonte les rivières écossaises jusqu’à leur source, du ruisseau au fleuve. Né à San Francisco en 1946, installé en Écosse en 1982 pour fonder le tout premier département de photographie plasticienne d’Europe à la Glasgow School of Art, il photographie avec une chambre de 1898, une seule prise par lieu, jamais deux. Scattered Waters, dont ce tirage du Forth, fut son exploration fondatrice, celle qui l’attacha à son pays d’adoption. Premier photographe élu à la RSA, en 2007.

Une Vénus rose, composée de tiroirs de commode et de coquillages, se recoiffe devant un miroir rond. Calum Colvin peint sur des objets du quotidien avant de les photographier, recomposant en volume les tableaux de Titien, mais aussi de Rubens, Etty, David Scott ou Canova ailleurs dans sa série. Sculpteur de formation avant d’obtenir un master en photographie au Royal College of Art de Londres, il compte Venus Anadyomene parmi les derniers tirages qu’il réalise encore en argentique couleur plutôt qu’en numérique.

Un ciel nocturne strié de traînées d’étoiles surplombe une lueur jaune à l’horizon. En 2002, Philip Braham achète un appareil Fujifilm 6×9 cm pour photographier la nuit à la lueur de la pleine lune, reflet différé du soleil sur le paysage. Chaque tirage de la série « Different Histories of Light » porte un lieu et une heure précise, tandis que la longue pose saisit aussi ces traînées d’étoiles, temps profond glissé dans l’instant présent. Diplômé de Duncan of Jordanstone, il reçoit le Morton Award de la RSA en 2009.

Trois poires reposent sur un compotier blanc, cernées de taches et d’éclaboussures noires. Nature Morte est une photogravure au polymère : un positif repeint à la gouache puis exposé sur plaque sensible, qui renverse une composition classique et minimaliste dans l’abstraction. Né à Selkirk, dans les Borders écossaises, Alfons Bytautas s’est formé à Édimbourg puis auprès de Stanley William Hayter, graveur britannique dont l’atelier parisien Atelier 17 forma des générations d’artistes modernes. Il a ensuite dirigé pendant trente ans l’atelier de gravure d’Edinburgh Printmakers.

Un mur de pierres empilées s’embrase contre la lumière déclinante des Hébrides. En 1991, Julie Brook s’installe seule dans une arche de pierre naturelle, sur la côte inhabitée de l’île de Jura. De cette solitude naissent ses Firestacks, des cairns qu’elle embrase à marée montante et que l’eau finit par renverser. Dessin, peinture et photographie prolongent ces rencontres éphémères pour les rendre accessibles au public. Elle vit aujourd’hui sur l’île de Skye.

Une fillette de huit ans pose, sérieuse, le regard de côté. Lady Constance Anne Montagu Douglas Scott (morte en 1970), fille du 6e duc et de la duchesse de Buccleuch, est photographiée ainsi vers 1885. Elle épousera en 1908 l’Honorable Douglas Halyburton Cairns. Le portrait, issu de la Collection Buccleuch, ouvre deux siècles d’archives familiales conservées à Dalkeith même.

Des feuilles d’érable, saisies en noir et blanc, se détachent d’un fond sombre. Norman McBeath photographie ce qu’il nomme « le brouillard du familier », cette manière dont l’habitude finit par voiler notre regard sur les lieux trop connus. Dans un jardin ordinaire, il cherche le détail qui réveille l’œil. Photographe et graveur formé à la psychologie, il vit à Édimbourg et a collaboré avec le poète irlandais Paul Muldoon, lauréat du prix Pulitzer, et la romancière britannique Jeanette Winterson, autrice des Oranges ne sont pas les seuls fruits.

Des panneaux de lin imprimés de ruines et brodés de perles pendent, suspendus à une tringle de bois. Leena Nammari, artiste palestinienne installée en Écosse, fut longtemps infirmière avant de se former à la gravure à Duncan of Jordanstone. …it can only be here… mêle photographie et impression textile pour raconter l’exil et l’attachement au lieu, tissant identité et engagement communautaire dans la même trame.

Trois pitons rocheux se dressent contre un ciel strié, saisis par un procédé vieux de cent cinquante ans. Alex Boyd grimpe les sommets écossais une chambre victorienne sur le dos et développe ses plaques de collodion humide sur place, entre deux rochers. Il photographie ainsi le Storr, formation rocheuse emblématique de l’île de Skye, en 2013. Le tirage rejoint les collections de la Royal Scottish Academy (RSA) la même année, don de l’artiste, qui fut également artiste en résidence de l’Académie sur les Cuillins, l’autre grand massif montagneux de l’île.

Sous les tubes fluorescents d’un gymnase, une forêt semble avoir poussé entre les lignes du terrain. Formée à la peinture, Wendy McMurdo devient l’une des précurseures de la retouche numérique, bien avant la création de Photoshop. The Games Hall met en scène cette confusion entre technologie, imagination et réalité. En 2018, la Royal Photographic Society l’a nommée parmi ses Cent héroïnes de la photographie.

 

L’exposition « PhotoDalkeith RSA200 » se tient à Dalkeith Palace, Dalkeith Country Park, à une vingtaine de minutes du centre d’Édimbourg, du 22 août au 27 septembre 2026 (vendredi-dimanche, 10h-16h), entrée 3£.

items.title: From Calotype to Pixel: 200 Years of Scottish Photography
items.content:
IN IMAGES

From Calotype to Pixel: 200 Years of Scottish Photography

Like this shot by Wendy McMurdo, Scottish photography has never stopped tampering with reality, the better to tell its country’s story. This summer, Dalkeith Palace, the historic seat of the Dukes of Buccleuch on the edge of Edinburgh, traces two centuries of the medium, from the pioneering calotypes of Hill & Adamson to today’s documentary practice, marking the bicentenary of the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA). A photographer-by-photographer tour of the show.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos: courtesy of PhotoDalkeith RSA200

Standing before his own paintings of tulips, Derrick Guild paints decorative patterns directly onto living tulips. Follower documents this performance, given at the RSA’s Annual Exhibition in 2016, in which the artist takes on the role of a follower of the Dutch Golden Age. The scene replays tulip mania, when a single flower could fetch ten times a skilled craftsman’s annual wage. Trained at Duncan of Jordanstone College of Art and Design in Dundee, Derrick Guild has since painted still lifes haunted by the Flemish and Dutch masters.

Daniel Cook immerses himself in the lives of his subjects for a practice that is at once documentary and fictional, giving voice to communities whose stories are too often left untold. Ricky Babes belongs to his series “Love Letters From Aberdeenshire”. Winner of the RSA’s Morton Award in 2019, he lives and works in Glasgow.

A fragment of nature, ribboned with blades of grass and a spider’s web, rendered almost abstract by the close-up. Matthew Dalziel and Louise Scullion have worked in collaboration since 1993, sculpting, filming and photographing a nature in flux. Their installation Migrator, created in 1997 for Heathrow Airport, remains one of their best-known public commissions. The duo write that they seek to “sensually reconnect the human body to the elemental earth.”

The artist’s painted face, somewhere between self-portrait and masquerade, embodies this Self Portrait Of Us All as the Devil. Graham Fagen represented Scotland at the Venice Biennale in 2015 with The Slave’s Lament, a video installation combining a poem by Robert Burns with the voice of reggae singer Ghetto Priest. Slavery, musical influence, the symbolic power of flowers: his works, often developed over long stretches of time with other collaborators, relentlessly probe national and personal identity.

A churning expanse of water, caught mid-storm, blurs the line between sky and sea. Since 1984, Thomas Joshua Cooper has been tracing Scottish rivers back to their source, from stream to river. Born in San Francisco in 1946, he settled in Scotland in 1982 to found Europe’s first fine art photography department, at the Glasgow School of Art, and photographs with an 1898 camera, one single exposure per site, never two. “Scattered Waters”, which includes this print of the Forth, was his foundational body of work, the one that bound him to his adopted country. He became the first photographer elected to the RSA, in 2007.

A pink Venus, built from chest-of-drawers and seashells, fixes her hair before a round mirror. Calum Colvin paints onto everyday objects before photographing them, reconstructing in three dimensions the paintings of Titian, and elsewhere in the series, of Rubens, Etty, David Scott or Canova. Trained as a sculptor before completing a master’s in photography at the Royal College of Art in London, he counts Venus Anadyomene among the last prints he made using traditional colour film rather than digital.

A night sky streaked with star trails hangs over a yellow glow on the horizon. In 2002, Philip Braham bought a 6x9cm Fujifilm camera to photograph landscapes at night by the light of the full moon, itself a delayed reflection of the sun. Each print in the “Different Histories of Light” series records a precise place and time, while the long exposure also captures those star trails, deep time slipped into a single instant. A graduate of Duncan of Jordanstone, he received the RSA’s Morton Award in 2009.

Three pears sit on a white compote dish, ringed by stains and splashes of black. Nature Morte is a polymer photogravure: a positive repainted in gouache and then exposed onto a light-sensitive plate, tipping a classical, minimalist composition into abstraction. Born in Selkirk, in the Scottish Borders, Alfons Bytautas trained in Edinburgh before studying under Stanley William Hayter, the British printmaker whose Paris workshop, Atelier 17, shaped generations of modern artists. He went on to run Edinburgh Printmakers’ workshop for thirty years.

A wall of stacked stones catches fire against the fading light of the Hebrides. In 1991, Julie Brook moved alone into a natural rock arch on the uninhabited west coast of the Isle of Jura. Out of that solitude came her “Firestacks”, cairns she sets alight as the tide comes in, until the water topples them. Drawing, painting and photography extend these fleeting encounters, making them accessible to audiences beyond the site itself. She now lives on the Isle of Skye.

An eight-year-old girl poses, solemn, gazing sideways. Lady Constance Anne Montagu Douglas Scott (d. 1970), daughter of the 6th Duke and Duchess of Buccleuch, was photographed thus around 1885. She would marry the Honourable Douglas Halyburton Cairns in 1908. The portrait, drawn from the Buccleuch Collection, opens onto two centuries of family archives still kept at Dalkeith itself.

Maple leaves, captured in black and white, stand out against a dark ground. Norman McBeath photographs what he calls “the fog of the familiar,” the way habit can veil our view of well-known surroundings. In an ordinary garden, he searches for the detail that jolts the eye awake. A photographer and printmaker trained in psychology, he lives in Edinburgh and has collaborated with the Irish poet Paul Muldoon, a Pulitzer Prize winner, and the British novelist Jeanette Winterson, author of Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit.

Panels of linen, printed with ruins and beaded with embroidery, hang from a wooden rod. Leena Nammari, a Palestinian artist based in Scotland, worked for years as a nurse before training in printmaking at Duncan of Jordanstone. …it can only be here… combines photography and textile printing to speak of exile and attachment to place, weaving identity and community engagement into a single thread.

Three rocky pinnacles rise against a streaked sky, captured through a process a century and a half old. Alex Boyd climbs Scottish summits with a Victorian camera on his back and develops his wet-plate collodion negatives on the spot, wedged between rocks. This is how he photographed the Storr, an iconic rock formation on the Isle of Skye, in 2013. The print entered the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA) collections that same year, a gift from the artist, who also served as the Academy’s artist in residence on the Cuillin, the island’s other great mountain range.

Under the fluorescent strip lights of a gymnasium, a forest seems to have sprung up between the court markings. Trained as a painter, Wendy McMurdo became one of the pioneers of digital retouching, well before Photoshop existed. The Games Hall stages this confusion between technology, imagination and reality. In 2018, the Royal Photographic Society named her among its Hundred Heroines of photography.


“PhotoDalkeith RSA200” runs at Dalkeith Palace, Dalkeith Country Park, roughly twenty minutes from central Edinburgh, from 22 August to 27 September 2026 (Friday to Sunday, 10am-4pm), admission £3.

Their installation Migrator, created in 1997 for Heathrow Airport, remains one of their best-known public commissions. The duo write that they seek to “sensually reconnect the human body to the elemental earth.”

The artist’s painted face, somewhere between self-portrait and masquerade, embodies this Self Portrait Of Us All as the Devil. Graham Fagen represented Scotland at the Venice Biennale in 2015 with The Slave’s Lament, a video installation combining a poem by Robert Burns with the voice of reggae singer Ghetto Priest. Slavery, musical influence, the symbolic power of flowers: his works, often developed over long stretches of time with other collaborators, relentlessly probe national and personal identity.

A churning expanse of water, caught mid-storm, blurs the line between sky and sea. Since 1984, Thomas Joshua Cooper has been tracing Scottish rivers back to their source, from stream to river. Born in San Francisco in 1946, he settled in Scotland in 1982 to found Europe’s first fine art photography department, at the Glasgow School of Art, and photographs with an 1898 camera, one single exposure per site, never two. “Scattered Waters”, which includes this print of the Forth, was his foundational body of work, the one that bound him to his adopted country. He became the first photographer elected to the RSA, in 2007.

A pink Venus, built from chest-of-drawers and seashells, fixes her hair before a round mirror. Calum Colvin paints onto everyday objects before photographing them, reconstructing in three dimensions the paintings of Titian, and elsewhere in the series, of Rubens, Etty, David Scott or Canova. Trained as a sculptor before completing a master’s in photography at the Royal College of Art in London, he counts Venus Anadyomene among the last prints he made using traditional colour film rather than digital.

A night sky streaked with star trails hangs over a yellow glow on the horizon. In 2002, Philip Braham bought a 6x9cm Fujifilm camera to photograph landscapes at night by the light of the full moon, itself a delayed reflection of the sun. Each print in the “Different Histories of Light” series records a precise place and time, while the long exposure also captures those star trails, deep time slipped into a single instant. A graduate of Duncan of Jordanstone, he received the RSA’s Morton Award in 2009.

Three pears sit on a white compote dish, ringed by stains and splashes of black. Nature Morte is a polymer photogravure: a positive repainted in gouache and then exposed onto a light-sensitive plate, tipping a classical, minimalist composition into abstraction. Born in Selkirk, in the Scottish Borders, Alfons Bytautas trained in Edinburgh before studying under Stanley William Hayter, the British printmaker whose Paris workshop, Atelier 17, shaped generations of modern artists. He went on to run Edinburgh Printmakers’ workshop for thirty years.

A wall of stacked stones catches fire against the fading light of the Hebrides. In 1991, Julie Brook moved alone into a natural rock arch on the uninhabited west coast of the Isle of Jura. Out of that solitude came her “Firestacks”, cairns she sets alight as the tide comes in, until the water topples them. Drawing, painting and photography extend these fleeting encounters, making them accessible to audiences beyond the site itself. She now lives on the Isle of Skye.

An eight-year-old girl poses, solemn, gazing sideways. Lady Constance Anne Montagu Douglas Scott (d. 1970), daughter of the 6th Duke and Duchess of Buccleuch, was photographed thus around 1885. She would marry the Honourable Douglas Halyburton Cairns in 1908. The portrait, drawn from the Buccleuch Collection, opens onto two centuries of family archives still kept at Dalkeith itself.

Maple leaves, captured in black and white, stand out against a dark ground. Norman McBeath photographs what he calls “the fog of the familiar,” the way habit can veil our view of well-known surroundings. In an ordinary garden, he searches for the detail that jolts the eye awake. A photographer and printmaker trained in psychology, he lives in Edinburgh and has collaborated with the Irish poet Paul Muldoon, a Pulitzer Prize winner, and the British novelist Jeanette Winterson, author of Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit.

Panels of linen, printed with ruins and beaded with embroidery, hang from a wooden rod. Leena Nammari, a Palestinian artist based in Scotland, worked for years as a nurse before training in printmaking at Duncan of Jordanstone. …it can only be here… combines photography and textile printing to speak of exile and attachment to place, weaving identity and community engagement into a single thread.

Three rocky pinnacles rise against a streaked sky, captured through a process a century and a half old. Alex Boyd climbs Scottish summits with a Victorian camera on his back and develops his wet-plate collodion negatives on the spot, wedged between rocks. This is how he photographed the Storr, an iconic rock formation on the Isle of Skye, in 2013. The print entered the Royal Scottish Academy (RSA) collections that same year, a gift from the artist, who also served as the Academy’s artist in residence on the Cuillin, the island’s other great mountain range.

Under the fluorescent strip lights of a gymnasium, a forest seems to have sprung up between the court markings. Trained as a painter, Wendy McMurdo became one of the pioneers of digital retouching, well before Photoshop existed. The Games Hall stages this confusion between technology, imagination and reality. In 2018, the Royal Photographic Society named her among its Hundred Heroines of photography.


“PhotoDalkeith RSA200” runs at Dalkeith Palace, Dalkeith Country Park, roughly twenty minutes from central Edinburgh, from 22 August to 27 September 2026 (Friday to Sunday, 10am-4pm), admission £3.

items.title: Bob Farese, l’eau sans horizon
items.content:
EN IMAGES

Bob Farese, l'eau sans horizon

Dans A Perfect Medium, publié chez MW Editions, le médecin et biologiste cellulaire Bob Farese, Jr. photographie l’eau sous toutes ses formes, et de si près que l’on s’y fond en perdant toute notion d’échelle, d’espace et de temps.

Par Guénola Pellen. Photos de Bob Farese, Jr.

Après l’air, l’eau est sans doute l’élément qui résiste le plus à la photographie. Difficilement saisissable, on la photographie en plongée sous-marine, lors d’événements sportifs (surf, voile) ou d’expéditions en mer. Plus souvent encore, on la photographie depuis le rivage ou le pont d’un bateau, en misant sur l’horizon pour la contextualiser et la cadrer, tant « les humains ont tendance à considérer l’eau comme quelque chose d’extérieur à eux-mêmes », comme l’observe Bob Farese dans son avant-propos.

En supprimant cette ligne d’horizon, le photographe supprime tout repère. Une gerbe d’écume devient sa propre architecture. Un glacier islandais révèle une texture semblable à un crayonné au fusain. Un banc de poissons revêt la texture d’une étoffe. L’information existe mais elle est limitée au strict minimum et reportée en fin de volume, avec une précision de cahier de laboratoire : lieu, heure, date.

Entre 2020 et 2025, Farese a photographié l’eau qui se trouvait devant lui. L’eau est tantôt celle de Paris, un soir de novembre, de Copenhague au matin ou de l’aquarium de Monterey Bay. Il n’y a aucun exploit dans ces images, aucune attente de la vague parfaite par le photographe.

Ce parti pris trouve son explication dans le parcours de Bob Farese, médecin et biologiste cellulaire qui travaille sur le métabolisme. « Je suis attiré par l’eau qui coule en nous », écrit-il. « Nous sommes, par essence, de l’eau. Environ 70 % de notre masse, mais plus de 99 % de nos molécules, sont de l’eau. »

Medium, le titre de son ouvrage, désigne le milieu vital autant que le support photographique, comme un écho au titre de son premier livre, Am I Not Light, déjà emprunté à la physique.

Au fil des pages, la contemplation bascule vers l’argument. « Polluer l’eau, c’est nous polluer nous-mêmes », assure l’auteur. « Empoisonner l’eau, c’est nous empoisonner nous-mêmes. Prendre soin de l’eau, c’est prendre soin de nous ». Si l’horizon a disparu de ces images, c’est aussi pour que l’on cesse de regarder l’eau de loin.


A Perfect Medium de Bob Farese, Jr., MW Editions, 144 pages, $50.

items.title: Water Without the Horizon
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Water Without the Horizon

In A Perfect Medium, published by MW Editions, physician and cell biologist Bob Farese, Jr. photographs water in all its guises, and from so close that the viewer dissolves into it, losing all sense of scale, space, and time.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Bob Farese, Jr.

After air, water is perhaps the element that most resists photography. Elusive by nature, it is typically captured underwater, at sporting events (surfing, sailing), or on expeditions at sea. More often still, it is photographed from the shore or the deck of a boat, relying on the horizon to give it context and composition for, as Farese observes in his foreword, “humans tend to think of water as something outside ourselves.”

By removing that horizon line, the photographer removes every point of reference. A burst of foam becomes its own architecture. An Icelandic glacier reveals a texture akin to charcoal shading. A school of fish takes on the grain of woven cloth. Information exists, but it is pared down to the essential and relegated to the back of the book, with the precision of a lab notebook: place, hour, date. 

Between 2020 and 2025, Farese photographed whatever water lay before him, sometimes in Paris on a November evening, sometimes in Copenhagen at dawn, sometimes at the Monterey Bay Aquarium. There is no feat of daring in these images, no waiting on the photographer’s part for the perfect wave.

This choice finds its explanation in Farese’s own path, a physician and cell biologist who studies metabolism. “I am drawn to the water that flows within us,” he writes. “We are, in essence, water. About 70 percent of our mass, but more than 99 percent of our molecules, are water.”

Medium, the title of his book, names both the vital element and the photographic support: an echo of the title of his first book, Am I Not Light, likewise borrowed from physics.

Page by page, contemplation tips over into argument. “To pollute water is to pollute ourselves,” the author affirms. “To poison water is to poison ourselves. So the simple truth is this: to care for water is to care for ourselves.” If the horizon has vanished from these images, it is also so that we might stop looking at water from a distance.


A Perfect Medium by Bob Farese, Jr., MW Editions, 144 pages, $50.

items.title: Guadalupe Laiz: “The Horse is a Reflection of Iceland”
items.content:
In the Land of Fire and Ice broadens the frame of your first book, moving from the horse alone to the horse within its environment. Was that a natural evolution, or a deliberate intention from the start?

Guadalupe Laiz: It was both. When I created Horses of Iceland, I was completely captivated by the horse itself: its character, its spirit, its expressions. But over time I realized that to truly understand the Icelandic horse, you cannot separate it from the land that shaped it. The horse is a reflection of Iceland. The resilience, the beauty, the unpredictability, the quiet strength. They belong to one another.

As I spent more time in the country, I felt compelled to widen the frame and tell a larger story. The landscape was no longer simply a backdrop; it became a character in its own right. This book became an exploration of that relationship, of how place shapes life and how life, in turn, becomes inseparable from place.

You worked with local breeders to transport horses to iconic locations: Skógafoss, the Fagradalsfjall volcano. How do you negotiate that kind of logistics, and how much room do you leave for the unexpected?

Projects like this require an enormous amount of planning, trust, and collaboration. Nothing happens alone. Local breeders and horse owners became essential partners, helping us safely bring horses into locations that are often difficult to access.

But more than partners I will call them friends, because I built reciprocal and organic relationships with them over the years. These relationships turned every trip into an organic collaboration where both, the owners and I worked our hardest for the very same goal: to showcase these majestic horses in the best way possible. 

But no matter how much planning goes into a photograph, nature always has the final word. I learned early on that if I become too attached to a specific outcome, I miss the moments that are actually unfolding in front of me. Some of my favorite photographs happened because conditions changed, weather arrived unexpectedly, or a horse reacted in a way I never anticipated.

I learned early on that if I become too attached to a specific outcome, I miss the moments that are actually unfolding in front of me. Some of my favorite photographs happened because conditions changed, weather arrived unexpectedly, or a horse reacted in a way I never anticipated.

The preparation gets you to the right place. The unexpected is what gives the image life.

Iceland is an extreme environment: raking light, brutal weather, difficult terrain. How does that shape the way you work, both technically and mentally?

Iceland teaches humility. There are days when the weather changes five times in an hour. Winds become so strong you can barely stand. Light appears for a few seconds and disappears just as quickly. Technically, it forces you to be prepared and adaptable. Mentally, it teaches patience and surrender.

I learned that the landscape does not care about my plans. The more I tried to control the experience, the more frustrated I became. The more I learned to work with the conditions rather than against them, the more rewarding the process became. Some of the strongest images in the book came from moments that initially felt like failures.

The drone footage brings an aerial perspective that ground-level photography simply cannot achieve. How did you think about the dialogue between your images and Kolbeinsson’s: two gazes and two altitudes for a same subject?

What I love about our collaboration is that we were telling the same story from different perspectives. My work often focuses on intimacy. I want to be close enough to feel the presence of the animal, to connect emotionally with it.

Kolbeinsson’s aerial imagery reveals something equally important: scale. From above, you begin to understand how horses move through the landscape and how deeply they belong to it. Neither perspective is complete on its own. Together they create a fuller understanding of Iceland, where the individual horse and the vastness of the land exist in constant conversation.

After five years of trips to Iceland for this single project, what does repetition change in the way you see the same animal and the same landscape?

At first, you photograph what is obvious. Then, if you stay long enough, you begin to notice what is subtle. Repetition strips away assumptions. It teaches you that a landscape is never truly the same, even if you return to the exact same place. The weather changes, the light changes, the season changes, and perhaps most importantly, you change.

Over five years, Iceland became less of a destination and more of a relationship. The photographs became less about documenting a place and more about listening to it. The longer I stayed, the less I felt I knew, and strangely, that opened the door to deeper work.

You work in both color and black and white. How do you choose between them? Is that a decision made in the field, or in the edit?

For me, that decision almost always happens during the edit. When color is essential to the emotional experience of the image, I keep it. Iceland offers extraordinary colors: volcanic reds, mossy greens, glacial blues, and dramatic skies.

Sometimes those colors are part of the story. But there are other moments when color becomes a distraction. Black and white allows me to focus on form, texture, movement, and emotion. It removes information and, in doing so, often reveals something deeper.

I don’t approach either as superior. They are simply different languages, and each photograph tells me which language it wants to speak.

Beneath the formal beauty, there is a dimension of conservation and witness. How do you carry both ambitions, the aesthetic and the documentary, without one overwhelming the other?

Beauty is often what invites people into a photograph. It creates a moment of connection. But if the work stops there, I feel I’ve missed an opportunity. My goal has never been to create beautiful images for their own sake. Beauty is the doorway. Beyond that doorway is a deeper conversation about our relationship with nature, what we stand to lose, and what still remains worth protecting.

I don’t separate aesthetics and conservation. For me, they are inseparable. People protect what they love, and they love what they feel connected to. If a photograph can create that connection, even for a moment, then it has the potential to become something more than an image. It becomes a reason to care. And in a world increasingly disconnected from the natural world, creating reasons to care feels more important than ever.

In the Land of Fire and Ice: Horses of Iceland by Guadalupe Laiz is published by Images Publishing, and is available at $125.
